content.title: About
content.content: Beef Stroganoff with noodles is a classic Russian dish featuring tender strips of beef simmered in a creamy mushroom sauce and served over boiled noodles. The combination of a rich sauce and hearty noodles makes it a favorite both at home and in restaurants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is named after Russian Count Stroganov, though the original recipe differs greatly from modern versions.
Traditional sauce is made with sour cream, tomato paste, and mushrooms, but regional variations add wine, mustard, or soy sauce.
Noodles served with Stroganoff are often egg noodles, but any pasta type—spaghetti, fettuccine, or rice noodles—can be used.
The dish became popular in the United States in the early 20th century, where it is commonly called “Stroganoff” and served with pasta.
A vegetarian version replaces beef with mushrooms while preserving the creamy flavor.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D from sour cream
items.content: The creamy sauce adds calcium and vitamin D, supporting bone health.

items.title: Mushrooms supply B‑vitamins
items.content: Mushrooms contribute vitamins B2, B3, and B5, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Carbohydrates from noodles provide energy
items.content: Boiled noodles deliver quick‑release carbs to maintain energy levels.

items.title: High in saturated fat
items.content: Cream and beef can raise cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The sauce often contains salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Sour cream may trigger reactions in those with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Digestive heaviness of red meat
items.content: Some individuals may experience discomfort due to the richness of beef.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the Stroganoff hot, ladling the sauce over the beef and noodles. Garnish with fresh parsley or dill and a pinch of black pepper. For a healthier twist, use whole‑grain pasta to increase fiber content.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat gently, bringing the sauce back to a gentle boil to prevent separation.

chicken-breast-grilled-without-sauce-ski.title: Chicken breast, grilled without sauce, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken breast is a lean cut of meat taken from the pectoral muscle of the bird. Grilled without sauce and without the skin, it retains a natural flavor and tender texture while being low in calories.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken breast contains less fat than other parts of the bird such as thighs or wings.
Grilling helps preserve more nutrients compared with deep‑frying.
It is one of the most affordable sources of complete protein.
Proper grilling creates a small amount of aromatic compounds that give a characteristic smoky taste.
Chicken breast is a staple in many diet plans and athletic nutrition programs.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 31 g of high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Skinless grilled breast contains less than 3 g of fat per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It is high in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support energy metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bone health, immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: Does not cause a rapid rise in blood glucose, beneficial for people monitoring blood sugar.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella; ensure internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

items.title: Bird meat allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content in marinades
items.content: If the breast is pre‑marinated, sodium levels can be high; choose low‑salt options.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the grilled breast for salads, wraps, soups, or use it as a protein base for bowls. It pairs well with vegetables, whole grains, and light sauces such as yogurt or lemon‑based dressings.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw breast in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C for up to 2 days. Cooked breast can be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days or frozen for up to 2 months.

corn-canned-reduced-sodium-cooked-with-b.title: Corn, canned, reduced sodium, cooked with butter or margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Canned corn with reduced sodium, cooked with butter or margarine, is a ready‑to‑eat vegetable product. It retains a sweet flavor and a crisp texture, while the lower salt content makes it suitable for low‑sodium diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn is one of the most widely canned vegetable crops worldwide.
Reduced sodium is achieved by replacing part of the salt with flavor enhancers and spices.
Cooking with butter or margarine enhances taste and improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
Canned corn stores for long periods without losing its flavor quality.
In the United States, over 30% of corn consumption comes from canned products.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Corn provides fiber that supports digestive health and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis, supporting nervous system function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in corn protect the eyes from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: The reduced salt level makes this product suitable for people monitoring blood pressure.

items.title: Fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: The added butter or margarine improves the absorption of vitamins A and E present in corn.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn.

items.title: Added fat content
items.content: The product contains butter or margarine, increasing its calorie count and saturated fat.

items.title: Bisphenol A in cans
items.content: Some can linings may contain BPA, which is recommended to be limited.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Corn can be eaten straight from the can, added to salads, soups, stews, or used as a side dish. It can also be quickly warmed in a skillet with a little extra butter for enhanced flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened can in a cool, dry place. After opening, keep the corn in a sealed container in the refrigerator and consume within 3–4 days. Discard if it develops an off odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Greens, canned, cooked is a blend of chopped leafy vegetables such as spinach, kale, broccoli and green peas that have been heat‑treated and sealed in airtight cans. The product is ready to eat without further cooking, retains most of its nutrients, and has a tender texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canned greens are often used in military rations and backpacking meals because of their long shelf life.
The "Greens" blend typically includes at least five different leafy vegetables, increasing the variety of vitamins and minerals.
Thermal processing destroys most microorganisms, allowing storage for up to three years at room temperature.
Canned vegetables are frequently fortified with a small amount of salt and antioxidants to preserve color and flavor.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Leafy greens provide B6, folate (B9) and riboflavin (B2), which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K supports blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Carotenoids and polyphenols protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from leafy vegetables promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Vegetables are low in calories, making them a good choice for weight management.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned greens often contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Vegetable allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to specific leafy vegetables.

items.title: BPA in packaging
items.content: Metal cans can have trace amounts of BPA; choose BPA‑free labeled products if this is a concern.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Greens can be eaten straight from the can, added to salads, soups, pasta, or omelets. They may be gently warmed in the microwave or on the stove, but this is optional.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the contents in a sealed container in the refrigerator and consume within 3‑5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Oolong is a semi‑oxidized tea made from the leaves of Camellia sinensis. It sits between green and black tea, offering a light fruity aroma and a gentle briskness. Served hot, it is typically brewed using whole leaves.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oolong originates from the Fujian province of China and Taiwan.
There are more than 30 varieties, each with distinct aromas ranging from floral to nutty.
The “twisting” technique of the leaves preserves natural flavors and makes brewing easier.
Oolong is often featured in tea ceremonies that value its evolving flavor profile over multiple infusions.
Aged oolongs, stored for several years, develop a deep, earthy character.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Oolong contains polyphenols that help combat free radicals and support cellular health.

items.title: Metabolism boost
items.content: Caffeine and catechins may increase metabolic rate and aid fat oxidation.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Regular moderate consumption can help lower LDL cholesterol levels.

items.title: Stress reduction
items.content: Aromatic compounds in oolong have calming effects, promoting relaxation.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Warm oolong stimulates gastric juice production, easing digestion.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Oolong contains caffeine; those sensitive should limit intake.

items.title: Iron absorption
items.content: Tannins may reduce iron absorption, so avoid drinking tea with iron supplements.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergy to tea components.

items.title: Water quality
items.content: Hard water can alter flavor and increase mineral content in the brew.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour hot water (80‑90 °C) over the leaf oolong and steep for 2‑3 minutes. Multiple infusions are possible, extending steep time slightly each round. Drink plain or with a touch of honey.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store oolong in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Keep it away from direct sunlight and moisture to prevent oxidation of the leaves.
